chunks: Al-Tawhid: Ibn al-Walid, from al-Saffar, from al-Yaqtini, from Ibn Abi Najran who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far the Second (peace be upon him) about Tawhid, saying: Should I imagine a thing? He said: Yes, (something) neither cognisable nor delimited. Whatever your imagination falls upon is different than He. Nothing is like Him and imaginations do not reach Him. How can imaginations reach Him when He is other than what can be cognised and other than what is represented in the imaginations? It is imagined something neither cognisable nor delimited.
ai.seo_question: How should one conceive of God if He cannot be fully understood or limited?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that while imagination is necessary to affirm God's existence, the mind's conceptualization is inherently limited and thus contrary to His infinite essence. This hadith underscores the Shia doctrine of *tanzih* (divine transcendence), emphasizing that any attribute or form conceived by human intellect is a negation of God's true reality, as He is beyond all sensory and intellectual perception. The narration highlights the paradox that we must use our limited faculties to point toward the Absolute, while simultaneously recognizing that the Absolute exceeds those faculties.
